[IMG: /graphics/8367448804fb9684aa1273c70015f13f]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
From the diagram, we can see that [MATH: \triangle{ABC}] is an equilateral triangle.

We're told that the perimeter of [MATH: \triangle ABC] is [MATH: p_1=21,] and since all [MATH: 3] sides have equal length, each side must have a length of [MATH: \dfrac{p_1}{3}= \dfrac{21}{3} = 7\,.]

So now we know that [MATH: AB=BC=AC = 7,] and we have enough information to compute the perimeter of the triangle [MATH: \triangle{ABD}\mathbin{:}] [MATH: p|= AB + BD + DA; = 7 + 3 + 7; = 17]

Therefore, the perimeter of [MATH: \triangle ABD] is [MATH: p=17.]

What is the perimeter of the pentagon?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The perimeter [MATH: p] of a polygon is the sum of the measures of all its sides. So, we can simply calculate

[MATH: p|= 25mm + 26mm + 30mm + 18mm + 21mm; = 120mm]

Finally, since the perimeter is a large quantity of [MATH: \textrm{mm},] we will convert to [MATH: \textrm{cm}\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: p = 120\, \mathrm{mm} = 12\,\mathrm{cm}.]

EXPLANATION

Explanation:
